claim: Two imagined households and the Visitor's choice are composite framing for Paris1783, not a recovered day's menu or a claim that all rich/poor people ate alike.
limit: No invented names, household accounts, exact daily budget or universal meal.

claim: Mercier describes abundant food at Les Halles and prominent pastry, charcuterie and roast-food displays in Paris.
limit: Availability in shops does not establish affordability for all; do not reproduce his precise counts or every-day guarantees.

claim: Mercier calls bread a principal food of the urban poor.
locator: Chapter631 paragraph beginning Le pain qu'on mange à Paris.
limit: Not their sole food, not a quantified calorie percentage; no modern nutrition equivalence.

claim: Mercier gives an example of a poor household whose small sausage purchase supplies its limited good fare, and argues small purchases can be costly.
locator: Chapter67 paragraph Plus les classes sont indigentes.
limit: One author's example, not a universal diet or measured representative family; no assertion the portion was all calories for a whole day.

claim: His account also names soup and boiled beef, evening beef dishes and Sunday mutton among ordinary Parisian meals.
limit: Do not turn his broad rhetorical population estimate into data or suggest these meals were within every destitute person's reach.

claim: The relevant comparison includes quantity, choice, preparation and access, not a rule that poor people ate no meat or that cabbage meant poverty.
locator: Ordinary-meal and sausage passages; Menon cabbage recipe.
limit: Synthesis of cited examples, not a claim of identical diets or an affordability index.

claim: Menon's1755cookbook lists roast poultry by season and explains spit preparation; poultry also appears in Mercier's roast-shop descriptions.
limit: Supports an illustrative affluent poultry dish, not a specific1783banquet menu or universal luxury item.

claim: Menon's cabbage recipe blanches, cools and squeezes the cabbage, then braises it and serves it around meat.
limit: Descriptive history, not modern recipe/safety advice; no unsourced exact cooking times.

claim: Its sauce uses ham,mushrooms,garlic with a clove,broth/coulis; it is reduced,strained and finished with pepper.
limit: Do not replace cabbage sauce with neighbouring cauliflower's butter recipe. No invented cream in this particular sauce.

claim: This recipe demonstrates that an ordinary vegetable can involve multiple ingredients,stages,fuel and skilled work; the finished plate hides some preparation.
limit: No measured labour hours,cost or assumption every wealthy household used this recipe.

claim: Mercier describes small households with limited hearths sending meat to pastry-shop ovens, partly to save wood; they pay for cooking.
limit: Modest households able to buy meat, not necessarily the poorest. No universal home-oven absence or exact charge schedule.

claim: Mercier says some wealthy-household servants ate better than modest bourgeois because lavish tables left food; this is his social observation.
locator: Chapter67 un laquais; chapter383 on service and food.
limit: Explicitly attributed, not every servant, not proof servants had more power or better lives than employers.

claim: Menon gives a rissoles recipe starting with leftover roast poultry, turning it into filling enclosed in thin pastry and fried as crescents.
locator: VolumeIII p26,Rissoles à la Béchamel; p27game alternative separately.
limit: Use poultry recipe only; do not claim all leftovers followed this route or identify it as a modern croquette.

claim: Mercier uses sharp social criticism and staged dialogue mocking wealthy diners' demands for novelty; this differs from a prescriptive cookbook. Neither supplies a whole society's actual menu or a single cause of revolution.
limit: No cake quotation, famine spectacle or claim dinner alone caused1789.
